subtopic_detail: prioritising which medicine to withdraw first after recurrent falls when there is no postural drop
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 79 year old man admitted after his second fall in six weeks. Both falls happened at home in the early hours when he got up to pass urine. He did not lose consciousness on either occasion and remembers hitting the floor.

His daughter has brought in his dose administration aid. He takes perindopril, amlodipine, temazepam nightly which he has taken for about six years, sertraline, aspirin, atorvastatin, metformin, pantoprazole, docusate and regular paracetamol. He drinks no alcohol. Lying and standing blood pressures have been recorded on the ward over two days.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, blood pressure 138/78, respiratory rate 15, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Timed up and go 18 seconds, no postural drop on repeated lying and standing measurement, no focal neurological deficit, mini mental state examination 28 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram sinus rhythm with normal intervals, 24 hour Holter monitor shows no pauses or arrhythmia, creatinine within normal limits, vitamin B12 and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: Which single medication change is the highest priority?

options.text: Stop pantoprazole, which has had no documented indication for six years
options.rationale: Indefinite proton pump inhibitor therapy without indication is worth unwinding and carries its own risks including fracture and hypomagnesaemia, but those act over years rather than explaining two falls in six weeks. It ranks below the sedative on urgency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Stop amlodipine and review the blood pressure in the clinic in two weeks
options.rationale: Withdrawing an antihypertensive is the reflex answer in a faller, but the lying and standing measurements were repeated and show no postural drop, which removes the mechanism this change would address. It would be correct if he had a symptomatic drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic on standing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Stop atorvastatin given his age and the absence of vascular disease
options.rationale: Reviewing a statin for ongoing benefit is a reasonable part of a broader medication review, but statins do not cause falls and stopping one changes nothing about tonight's risk. Deprescribing is prioritised by harm, and this drug is not the one causing harm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Wean and cease the nightly temazepam over the next four to eight weeks
options.rationale: Long term benzodiazepine use is among the strongest modifiable medication risks for falls and hip fracture in older people, and the nocturnal timing of both falls fits residual sedation on rising. Abrupt cessation after six years risks withdrawal, so a structured taper is the correct method. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Stop aspirin as primary prevention and review in the clinic in two weeks
options.rationale: Aspirin for primary prevention in this age group has an unfavourable balance of bleeding against benefit and is a fair target for review, particularly in someone who is falling. It reduces the consequence of a fall rather than the chance of one, so it is second order here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Medication review after a fall is most useful when it is prioritised rather than exhaustive, and the drug classes with the strongest causal link to falls are benzodiazepines and Z drugs, antipsychotics, antidepressants, opioids and anticholinergics, collectively described as fall risk increasing drugs. Orthostatic hypotension is the other major reversible contributor, but it must be demonstrated rather than assumed, because withdrawing antihypertensives from an older person who does not have a postural drop exposes them to cardiovascular risk for no fall benefit. Benzodiazepine withdrawal after years of use requires a gradual taper, typically reducing by about an eighth to a quarter of the dose every one to two weeks with slower steps at the end, and it is helped by explaining that the drug has long since stopped improving sleep architecture. A structured falls assessment should run in parallel, covering vision, footwear, home hazards, vitamin D and strength and balance exercise. Sertraline is also a fall risk increasing drug and is a legitimate second target once the sedative is addressed.
key_points: Benzodiazepines, Z drugs, antipsychotics, antidepressants, opioids and anticholinergics are the main fall risk increasing drugs
Demonstrate orthostatic hypotension before withdrawing antihypertensives in a faller
Taper long term benzodiazepines rather than ceasing abruptly
Prioritise deprescribing by the harm actually operating, not by list length
Run a structured falls assessment covering vision, footwear, home hazards and exercise alongside the medication change
explanation.pearls: Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes of standing; without that measured drop, stopping an antihypertensive after a fall treats a mechanism that has not been shown to exist.

subtopic_detail: changing opioid and route when the oral route fails and renal function is deteriorating at the end of life
stem:
You are the registrar on the community palliative care service visiting a 68 year old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer at home. Her pain has been well controlled on modified release oral morphine 60 mg twice daily for the past two months.

Over the past three days she has vomited after most doses and has not reliably kept a tablet down. Her husband says she has become much drowsier and that her hands and arms twitch in short jerks when she dozes, which is new. Bloods were taken yesterday by the visiting nurse. She wishes to remain at home and a subcutaneous syringe driver is available through the service.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 104/64, respiratory rate 12, SpO2 95 per cent in air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Rousable to voice, multifocal myoclonic jerks of the upper limbs, pinpoint pupils, abdomen soft with hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 218 micromol/L (60 to 110), estimated glomerular filtration rate 22 mL/min/1.73m2 (greater than 60), corrected calcium within normal limits, sodium within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her analgesia?

options.text: Convert to a continuous subcutaneous morphine infusion at the same daily dose
options.rationale: Changing route solves the vomiting but keeps the drug whose active metabolites are accumulating. Morphine 6 glucuronide is renally cleared and is the direct cause of the myoclonus and sedation, so this option would relieve one problem while worsening the other. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Increase the oral morphine dose and add regular oral metoclopramide
options.rationale: Drowsiness with myoclonus and pinpoint pupils indicates too much opioid effect rather than too little, so increasing the dose accelerates the toxicity. Her pain was controlled until the route failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Apply a transdermal fentanyl patch today and stop all other opioid therapy
options.rationale: Fentanyl is metabolically a sound choice in renal impairment, so the drug is not the error here. The patch takes twelve to twenty four hours to reach useful concentrations and cannot be titrated quickly, which makes it unsuitable when pain control must be maintained from today and the clinical situation is changing. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue oral morphine and add subcutaneous haloperidol for the vomiting
options.rationale: An antiemetic is appropriate alongside whatever opioid is chosen, but she is not absorbing the tablets, so continuing the oral route leaves her analgesia unreliable. It also leaves the accumulating metabolite in place. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Convert to a continuous subcutaneous hydromorphone infusion at a reduced dose
options.rationale: Hydromorphone has a far smaller burden of renally cleared active metabolite than morphine, which makes it the preferred switch when the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls and neurotoxicity has appeared. The dose is reduced below strict equianalgesic calculation because cross tolerance between opioids is incomplete. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

explanation.summary: Opioid rotation is prompted either by inadequate analgesia despite titration or, as here, by dose limiting toxicity, and declining renal function at the end of life is the commonest trigger in practice. Morphine is metabolised to morphine 3 glucuronide and morphine 6 glucuronide, both renally cleared, and their accumulation produces the recognisable picture of increasing sedation, multifocal myoclonus, pinpoint pupils and sometimes hyperalgesia or delirium. Hydromorphone and fentanyl carry a much lighter metabolite load and are the preferred agents once the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls below about 30 mL/min/1.73m2. Because cross tolerance between opioids is incomplete, the calculated equianalgesic dose is reduced, conventionally by around a quarter to a half, with breakthrough doses written and the patient reviewed within twenty four hours. A continuous subcutaneous infusion through a syringe driver is the standard way to deliver this at home when swallowing fails, and it allows antiemetic and anxiolytic to be combined in the same device.
key_points: Renally cleared morphine metabolites cause sedation, multifocal myoclonus and pinpoint pupils
Switch to hydromorphone or fentanyl when the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls below about 30 mL/min/1.73m2
Reduce the calculated equianalgesic dose because cross tolerance between opioids is incomplete
A subcutaneous syringe driver maintains analgesia when the oral route fails at home
Rising sedation with myoclonus signals opioid excess, not undertreated pain
explanation.pearls: New multifocal myoclonus in a patient stable on morphine is opioid neurotoxicity from metabolite accumulation until proven otherwise, and it should trigger a check of renal function and a switch of opioid rather than a dose increase.

subtopic_detail: choosing the starting corticosteroid dose for girdle pain when cranial arteritis features are absent
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 71 year old woman with six weeks of aching and stiffness across both shoulders and both hips. She is worst on waking and says it takes about two hours before she can move freely. She has been unable to lift her arms high enough to brush her own hair or to reach a shelf above her head.

She has taken atorvastatin for three years without previous problems. She has no jaw pain on chewing, no scalp tenderness and no visual symptoms, and her temporal arteries are not tender or thickened. There is no swelling of the small joints of her hands.

data_table.Examination: Painful restriction of active shoulder and hip abduction with full passive range, no synovitis of the hands or wrists, temporal arteries non tender with normal pulsation
data_table.Investigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 68 mm/h (less than 30), C reactive protein 54 mg/L (less than 5), creatine kinase within normal limits, rheumatoid factor negative, anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody negative, thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence prednisolone 15 mg daily and review the response in one week
options.rationale: Bilateral girdle pain with prolonged morning stiffness, raised inflammatory markers and normal muscle enzymes in this age group is treated with low dose corticosteroid, and a dose in the 12.5 to 25 mg range is the accepted starting point. The dramatic response within days is itself part of the diagnostic assessment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Cease atorvastatin and review the symptoms in the clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: Statin associated muscle symptoms would be a reasonable consideration, but a creatine kinase within normal limits alongside a markedly raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C reactive protein points away from a myopathy, since statin muscle injury does not raise inflammatory markers. Six weeks of observation also leaves her functionally disabled. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence prednisolone 50 mg daily and refer for temporal artery biopsy
options.rationale: High dose corticosteroid with urgent biopsy is the pathway when cranial arteritis is suspected, signalled by jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, temporal artery abnormality or any visual symptom. None of those is present, and this dose commits her to the toxicity of high dose steroid without the indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence weekly methotrexate 10 mg with folic acid supplementation
options.rationale: Methotrexate is used as a steroid sparing agent for relapsing disease or where corticosteroid toxicity is a particular concern, not as initial monotherapy. It works too slowly to address her current disability. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Commence regular naproxen 500 mg twice daily and refer to physiotherapy
options.rationale: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs give only partial relief in this condition and carry gastrointestinal and renal risk in her age group. A failure to respond to them is sometimes what delays the correct diagnosis for months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Girdle pain with prolonged morning stiffness and raised inflammatory markers in a patient over 50 is a clinical diagnosis supported by the exclusion of mimics rather than by any confirmatory test. The important mimics are inflammatory myopathy, which raises creatine kinase, late onset seronegative rheumatoid arthritis, which produces peripheral synovitis, hypothyroidism and statin myopathy, and each is addressed by a small targeted panel rather than a broad screen. The cardinal linked concern is cranial arteritis, which shares the underlying vasculopathy and occurs in a substantial minority, and any jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, temporal artery abnormality or visual disturbance mandates immediate high dose corticosteroid before biopsy because vision loss is irreversible. Treatment response is expected to be rapid and near complete within a few days, and a poor response should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis rather than dose escalation. Tapering is slow over one to two years with bone protection and monitoring for steroid related harm.
key_points: Start at 12.5 to 25 mg prednisolone daily for isolated girdle disease
A creatine kinase within normal limits argues against statin myopathy and inflammatory myositis
Jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual symptoms demand high dose steroid immediately
A poor response within a week should prompt diagnostic review rather than dose escalation
Plan bone protection and a slow taper over one to two years
explanation.pearls: Expect near complete relief within three to five days of starting prednisolone 15 mg daily; failure to respond by one week is a diagnostic red flag that should send you back to myositis, malignancy or late onset seronegative rheumatoid arthritis rather than upward on the dose.
